screens.title: Tilemaps & Level Design
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll learn why Unity's Tilemap system is central to building 2D levels quickly and reliably. Tilemaps let you paint grid-based environments much like drawing with pixels, but each painted tile can carry rendering, physics, and behavior. You'll see how a Grid defines cell size and structure, how Tilemaps become layers such as ground or background, and how a Tile Palette becomes your toolbox of paintable Tile assets. We'll also walk through practical steps: creating a Grid and multiple Tilemap children, building a Tile Palette from a sliced tileset, painting layers, and enabling collision with TilemapCollider2D and CompositeCollider2D for performance. Along the way we'll explore Rule Tiles for edge blending, Animated Tiles for moving water, and the idea of custom Scriptable Tiles for advanced behaviors. This matters because painting with tiles speeds iteration, keeps asset organization clean, and produces predictable physics and rendering behavior. A quick example: by painting a ground Tilemap and adding a TilemapCollider2D plus a CompositeCollider2D, your player will collide with terrain as a single optimized collider. Keep an eye out for common mistakes, like forgetting to select the active Tilemap or mismatched pixels-per-unit. Ready to build a small platformer section step-by-step and understand the why behind each step?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will explain the purpose of Unity's Tilemap system and why a Grid plus Tilemap children is the right pattern for layered 2D scenes. For example, you will recognize why keeping background art on a separate Tilemap keeps sorting and draw order predictable. Second, you will create and manage Tile Palettes and generate Tile assets from a sliced tileset. You'll build a palette asset, drag sprites into it, and save each tile for painting. Third, you will paint and erase tiles to construct multi-layered levels and assign sorting layers so background and foreground render correctly. Practically, this reduces manual sprite placement and speeds iteration. Fourth, you will implement collision by adding TilemapCollider2D and then optimize it by enabling Used By Composite and adding a CompositeCollider2D, reducing per-tile colliders into a single shape. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can check your work. These skills matter because they let you iterate levels quickly, avoid common collision pitfalls, and keep performance manageable as your map grows.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Continued
screens.narratorSegment: These additional objectives focus on advanced Tilemap features and safe design practices. First, you will identify when to use Rule Tiles to automatically adapt sprites based on neighbors, such as auto-connecting terrain edges, which significantly reduces manual edge painting. A concrete example is a grass tile that switches to an edge sprite when no neighboring grass tile exists on the left. Second, you will create Animated Tiles for repeating motion like flowing water, assigning a sequence of sprites and an animation speed so the Tile animates in-game. Third, you will understand the role of Scriptable Tiles, and the basics of creating a custom tile class that inherits from TileBase, which is useful when you need custom placement logic or tile-triggered behavior. Fourth, you will learn practical safeguards: check Pixels Per Unit on your sliced sprites, confirm the active Tilemap before painting, set Sorting Layers, and save often to avoid accidental overwrites. Each of these skills improves speed, visual consistency, and runtime performance. Practice these milestones in the hands-on activity to lock in the workflow for production-ready 2D level design.

screens.title: What is the Tilemap System?
screens.narratorSegment: A Tilemap system is Unity's specialized workflow and set of components for building grid-based 2D levels by painting tiles rather than placing individual sprites. At its core, a Grid GameObject defines the overall grid layout — cell size and spacing — while Tilemap child GameObjects store tile data for specific layers like ground, background, or foreground. Each Tilemap has a Tilemap Renderer that draws its tiles and can be assigned to a Sorting Layer so rendering order is predictable. The practical benefit is huge: painting a repeated floor pattern, or adding decorative elements, becomes fast and consistent, and tiles can carry physics or animation. For example, in a platformer you might create one Tilemap called GroundTilemap for collision and another called BackgroundTilemap for parallax art; each uses the same Grid so alignment is consistent. A common misconception is treating Tilemaps like simple sprites; instead, think of them as data layers that combine visual sprites with optional runtime behavior such as colliders or scripted logic. Key takeaway: Tilemaps turn repetitive level construction into a paint workflow that keeps art, physics, and layering organized and easy to iterate.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Tilemaps are paintable layers within a Grid that hold tile data, rendering settings, and optional physics for efficient 2D level construction.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › What is the Tilemap System?
Definition

Tilemap System

A workflow in Unity that uses a parent Grid and child Tilemaps to paint grid-based environments. Tilemaps hold tiles, while the Grid defines alignment and size.

Example
Use a single Grid with GroundTilemap for collision and BackgroundTilemap for art so everything lines up automatically.
Common misconception
Tilemaps are not just tiled sprites. They are data containers that can include colliders, animations, and script-driven behavior.
Why it matters
Painting tiles is faster, more consistent, and easier to maintain than placing individual sprites for large or repeating environments.
Visual: Layered cards
Grid
Defines cell size and alignment for child Tilemaps.
Tilemap
Child GameObject that holds tile data for a specific layer.
Tile Palette
Editor window where Tile assets are created and selected for painting.
Key Takeaway

Think of Tilemaps as paintable data layers that combine visuals, physics, and behaviors for fast level creation.

screens.title: Creating a Grid and Tilemap Children
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a Grid and Tilemap children is the first practical step to paint a level that aligns perfectly. Start by creating a Grid GameObject via the editor's GameObject menu and choosing 2D Object → Tilemap. Unity creates a Grid with a Tilemap child and a Tilemap Renderer component. The Grid controls cell size and cell gap; for pixel-art tiles you typically set the Grid cell size to match your sprite's Pixels Per Unit so tiles snap neatly. Next, add additional Tilemap children for different layers: rename the default to GroundTilemap, then add another child and call it BackgroundTilemap. Use separate Tilemaps to control ordering and collisions; GroundTilemap will often host physics and colliders while BackgroundTilemap remains purely visual. A common error is painting on the Scene without the intended Tilemap selected in the Hierarchy; always confirm the active Tilemap before painting. Finally, set Sorting Layers on each Tilemap's Tilemap Renderer — for example, Background behind Platforms — so draw order is correct. Following this disciplined setup avoids alignment problems and keeps your project organized as levels grow. Creating a Grid and Tilemap Children means create grid → create tilemap children, rename layers, match cell size to pixels per unit, and set sorting layers for clear draw order.. In practical terms, step-by-step setup for consistent alignment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Creating a Grid and Tilemap Children
Steps
  1. Create Grid: GameObject → 2D Object → Tilemap. Unity makes a Grid with a Tilemap child.
  2. Rename layers: Rename child to GroundTilemap; add another child for BackgroundTilemap.
  3. Match cell size: Set Grid cell size and verify Pixels Per Unit on sprites for clean snapping.
  4. Set Sorting Layers: Assign Background and Platforms layers on each Tilemap Renderer.
  5. Select active Tilemap: Always choose the Tilemap in Hierarchy before painting in Scene.
Scenario
In a platformer, GroundTilemap holds colliders and platforms while BackgroundTilemap holds distant parallax art using the same Grid to keep alignment.
Visual checklist
Grid cell size
Confirm cell size equals sprite PPU mapping for predictable placement.
Layers named
Use clear names like GroundTilemap, BackgroundTilemap for easy editing.
Select active Tilemap
If painting does nothing, re-select the Tilemap in the Hierarchy and try again.
Key Takeaway

A disciplined Grid + named Tilemap children workflow prevents alignment and ordering errors as your level scales.

screens.title: Creating a Tile Palette & Tile Assets
screens.narratorSegment: A Tile Palette is your toolbox of paintable tiles. To create one, open Window → 2D → Tile Palette and click Create New Palette. Name it, for example, PlatformerTiles, and save it as an asset in your project. Next, prepare your tileset by importing a tileset image, setting Sprite Mode to Multiple, and slicing it in the Sprite Editor using Grid By Cell Size. Make sure Pixels Per Unit matches your intended Grid cell size. Then drag the sliced sprites from the Project window into the Tile Palette window. Unity prompts you to save each sprite as a Tile asset; accept and save them. You can create Animated Tiles or Rule Tiles from the Create menu if you need motion or neighbor-aware sprites. A practical tip: group tiles in the palette by usage — terrain, decorations, hazards — so painting is faster. A common mistake is forgetting to save the Palette asset before painting; if the palette is not saved, tile assets might not be created persistently. By the end of this workflow you'll have a Palette populated with Tile assets, ready for the brush, fill, and erase tools in the Tile Palette window.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Creating a Tile Palette
Quick steps
  1. Create Palette: Window → 2D → Tile Palette → Create New Palette → Save as asset.
  2. Import tileset: Set Sprite Mode to Multiple and slice using Sprite Editor with the correct cell size.
  3. Drag slices into Palette: Save each generated Tile asset when prompted.
  4. Organize: Group tiles by function in the palette for faster painting.
Editor checklist
  • Pixels Per Unit matches Grid cell size.
  • Palette asset is saved inside Assets.
  • Slices are named consistently for ease of lookup.
Example: Slicing
If your tiles are 16x16 pixels and you want one Unity unit per tile, set Pixels Per Unit to 16 before slicing.

screens.title: Painting Tools: Brush, Fill, Erase
screens.narratorSegment: Painting a level is the tactile part of Tilemap design. The Tile Palette offers three primary tools you'll use constantly: the brush, fill, and erase tools. The brush paints individual tiles or click-drag strokes; use it for placing platforms and decorations precisely. The fill tool fills contiguous areas with the selected tile, which is handy for creating large ground masses quickly. The erase tool removes tiles from the active Tilemap. Always ensure the correct Tilemap is selected in the Hierarchy because painting acts on the active Tilemap — a very common error is painting on a different layer or seeing no change because an inactive Tilemap was selected. When you paint ground tiles intended for collisions, remember to add the TilemapCollider2D to that Tilemap; painting more tiles will update the collider set. Another practical tip: use smaller brush sizes for details and the fill tool for the broad strokes, then erase where needed to shape platforms. After painting, run the game to validate that the player interacts with the painted ground as expected; if not, check that the Tilemap has a collider and that the Sorting Layer is correct. Try painting a small platform, add TilemapCollider2D, and jump on it to confirm behavior.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Painting Tools
Tools
Brush: Paint single tiles or drag to draw lines. Use for platforms and details.
Fill: Fill contiguous areas quickly—ideal for ground bases.
Erase: Remove tiles from active Tilemap for corrections.
Common mistake
Painting does nothing because the wrong Tilemap is selected. Always select the intended Tilemap in the Hierarchy before painting.
Mini exercise
Paint a ground platform: choose a ground tile, set the active Tilemap to GroundTilemap, use brush to paint a 6x1 platform, then add a few 2x1 floating platforms.
Validation
After painting, add TilemapCollider2D to GroundTilemap and run the scene to confirm your player can stand and jump on the painted tiles.
Key Takeaway

Mix brush and fill for fast layout, then refine with erase. Confirm active Tilemap and colliders to avoid surprises.

screens.title: Adding TilemapCollider2D for Physics
screens.narratorSegment: When you want physics interactions with your painted ground, add a TilemapCollider2D component to the Tilemap GameObject that holds those tiles. The TilemapCollider2D inspects the tiles painted on its Tilemap and creates per-tile colliders, typically box-shaped, so a Rigidbody2D-based player can stand on or collide with them. This automatic generation is convenient but can become costly for large contiguous areas because it produces many individual colliders. One common pitfall is forgetting to add this component to the ground Tilemap and wondering why the player falls through. Another pitfall is leaving many individual colliders active in a large level, which increases physics workload. The recommended pattern is to enable Used By Composite on the TilemapCollider2D and then add a CompositeCollider2D to the same GameObject; Unity will then merge many small colliders into a single composite shape, drastically reducing physics overhead. Implementation note: adding a CompositeCollider2D often requires adding a Rigidbody2D and setting it to Static so the composite shape participates correctly. Always test performance after painting large areas and consider chunking very large worlds into multiple scenes to keep physics manageable.

keyIdea.title: Collider basics
keyIdea.text: TilemapCollider2D creates colliders from painted tiles; enable Used By Composite and add CompositeCollider2D to optimize many colliders into one shape.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › TilemapCollider2D
How it works
  • TilemapCollider2D examines painted tiles and generates colliders per tile.
  • For large contiguous tiles this can create many colliders and slow physics.
  • Enable Used By Composite on TilemapCollider2D and add CompositeCollider2D to merge colliders.
  • CompositeCollider2D typically requires a Rigidbody2D set to Static for proper behavior.
Practical check
If physics is slow on a large level, check how many separate colliders are present and add a CompositeCollider2D to optimize.
Example setup
Inspector steps:
  1. Add TilemapCollider2D to GroundTilemap.
  2. Check Used By Composite on TilemapCollider2D.
  3. Add CompositeCollider2D to GroundTilemap and add a Rigidbody2D set to Static when prompted.
Key Takeaway

Use CompositeCollider2D with Used By Composite to convert many per-tile colliders into a single efficient shape for performance.

screens.title: Per-tile colliders vs CompositeCollider2D
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the trade-offs between per-tile colliders and a CompositeCollider2D is essential for performance. By default, TilemapCollider2D generates an individual collider for each painted tile. This is simple and flexible, but on large contiguous ground areas it can create thousands of colliders, increasing physics calculations and reducing frame rate. The alternative is to check Used By Composite on the TilemapCollider2D and add a CompositeCollider2D. The composite merges those many colliders into larger contiguous shapes, dramatically reducing the number of collision checks. However, the composite shape can be slightly less accurate for isolated small tiles or tile-by-tile interactions that depend on per-tile segmentation. A practical guideline: use per-tile colliders during early prototyping for clarity, but switch to CompositeCollider2D for solid ground layers in larger or performance-sensitive levels. Also remember to set the Rigidbody2D to Static on the GameObject with the CompositeCollider2D. A common mistake is enabling composite but forgetting to check Used By Composite, which leaves the many per-tile colliders active. Test your level: if you see physics stutter on large maps, the composite is likely the right solution. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Per-tile vs Composite
Per-tile Colliders
Generates individual colliders for every painted tile. Highly precise for small, interactive tiles.
Pros: simple, exact. Cons: many colliders cause physics overhead on large maps.
When to use
Small maps or tiles where per-tile collision behavior is required.
CompositeCollider2D
Merges many small colliders into a single optimized shape when Used By Composite is enabled on the TilemapCollider2D.
Pros: performance. Cons: slightly less per-tile segmentation.
When to use
Large contiguous ground layers and production builds where physics performance matters.
Key Takeaway

Prototype with per-tile colliders if helpful; convert solid ground to CompositeCollider2D before shipping to reduce physics cost.

screens.title: Rule Tiles: Automating Terrain Connections
screens.narratorSegment: Rule Tiles let you define neighbor-based rules so a tile chooses the correct sprite depending on surrounding tiles. Instead of placing different edge or corner sprites manually, you create a Rule Tile and define rules like: use the center sprite when surrounded, use an edge sprite when no neighbor exists on the left, or use a corner sprite in L-shaped configurations. This automation is extremely useful for terrain that must visually connect, such as grass meeting dirt or stone paths. A concrete example: a grass Rule Tile might show a full grass tile when there are grass neighbors on all sides but automatically switch to a left-edge sprite when there is no grass to the left. Rule Tiles accelerate painting because the correct sprite is chosen at paint time based on local context. A common misconception is that Rule Tiles limit control — in fact, they increase consistency and reduce human error, while still allowing manual override if you need a special tile placement. Use Rule Tiles for large areas with repeating connection logic and save time while keeping art consistent across the map.

How Rule Tiles work
Define rules based on neighbor presence to automatically pick the correct sprite — edges, corners, and transitions.
Example: grass tile shows an edge sprite when there is no grass to the left.
When to use
Use Rule Tiles for terrain that must connect consistently and for large areas where manual edge management is tedious.
Practical steps
Create → Create → 2D → Tiles → Rule Tile. Define rules with neighbor positions and assign sprites for each case. Paint from the Tile Palette as usual.

Rule Tiles save time and avoid visual seams by automatically choosing edge and corner sprites based on neighbors.

screens.title: Animated Tiles & Bringing Levels to Life
screens.narratorSegment: Animated Tiles let you assign a sequence of sprites and an animation speed so a tile cycles through frames in the Tilemap. This is ideal for water, lava, torches, or any surface that should exhibit simple looping motion. To create one, use Create → 2D → Tiles → Animated Tile, then assign a set of sprites and a speed parameter. When painted, the Animated Tile will render its frame sequence at runtime without requiring separate Animator objects or spritesheets. Use Animated Tiles sparingly on large maps because many animated tiles can increase rendering work; reserve them for surfaces that benefit from motion. An example: create an Animated Tile for a water tile with three sprites and a moderate speed so the water appears to flow. A misconception is that animated tiles are heavy like full skeletal animations — they are simple sprite swaps driven by the Tile asset and are efficient for many common cases. The takeaway: Animated Tiles give motion without additional animator overhead, but monitor performance if you animate many tiles simultaneously. screens.title: Scriptable Tiles & Custom Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Scriptable Tiles let you implement custom placement or runtime behavior by creating a C# class that inherits from TileBase. This is an advanced technique for cases where a tile must perform logic when placed, removed, or when an actor interacts with it — for example, a pressure plate tile that triggers an event when the player stands on it. The chapter notes that you can create your own C# scripts inheriting from TileBase; do this carefully because custom code introduces maintenance and compatibility concerns. A minimal safe example is defining a class header that inherits TileBase and then implementing only the methods you need for drawing or providing tile data. Avoid embedding heavy runtime logic directly in tile data; prefer raising events that other components handle. An important practical step is testing your Scriptable Tile in the editor by placing and removing instances to confirm behavior and saving frequently. Misconception check: Scriptable Tiles are not required for most projects — use them only when the built-in Tile types (Tile, Rule Tile, Animated Tile) cannot express the behavior you need. When to use
Use Scriptable Tiles when you need custom placement logic or a tile that triggers behavior on interaction, beyond Rule or Animated Tiles.
Example: a pressure-plate tile that raises a gate when walked on.
Safety checklist
  • Keep tile logic small; raise events rather than embed heavy state machines.
  • Test placement and removal in editor frequently.
  • Document tile behaviors for team members.
Minimal class example
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.Tilemaps;

public class CustomTile : TileBase
{
  // Implement the minimal overrides you need,
  // such as GetTileData to provide the sprite and properties.
}
Pro tip

Prefer using built-in Tile types until you have a clear need for custom behavior; custom tiles increase maintenance cost.

screens.title: Hands-on: Build a Basic Platformer Level
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks you through building a small platformer section with Tilemaps. Start from a project with a sliced tileset saved as PlatformerTileset. png and ensure sprites are sliced with the expected Pixels Per Unit. Step 1: Create a Grid and a Tilemap child via GameObject → 2D Object → Tilemap. Rename the child GroundTilemap. Step 2: Add another Tilemap child named BackgroundTilemap and set Sorting Layers: Background for background, Platforms for ground. Step 3: Open Window → 2D → Tile Palette. Create a new palette named PlatformerTiles and drag your sliced sprites into it, saving Tile assets when prompted. Step 4: Select GroundTilemap and paint a simple ground base with the brush or fill tool, then add a few floating platforms. Step 5: Add a TilemapCollider2D to GroundTilemap, check Used By Composite, then add a CompositeCollider2D and accept creating a Rigidbody2D set to Static. Step 6: Select BackgroundTilemap and paint background elements. Step 7: Play the scene to verify the player can stand and jump on the painted ground. Checkpoints: verify PPU alignment, active Tilemap selection before painting, and that Collider + Composite settings improve physics. Save frequently.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll learn why Unity's Tilemap system is central to building 2D levels quickly and reliably. Tilemaps let you paint grid-based environments much like drawing with pixels, but each painted tile can carry rendering, physics, and behavior. You'll see how a Grid defines cell size and structure, how Tilemaps become layers such as ground or background, and how a Tile Palette becomes your toolbox of paintable Tile assets. We'll also walk through practical steps: creating a Grid and multiple Tilemap children, building a Tile Palette from a sliced tileset, painting layers, and enabling collision with TilemapCollider2D and CompositeCollider2D for performance. Along the way we'll explore Rule Tiles for edge blending, Animated Tiles for moving water, and the idea of custom Scriptable Tiles for advanced behaviors. This matters because painting with tiles speeds iteration, keeps asset organization clean, and produces predictable physics and rendering behavior. A quick example: by painting a ground Tilemap and adding a TilemapCollider2D plus a CompositeCollider2D, your player will collide with terrain as a single optimized collider. Keep an eye out for common mistakes, like forgetting to select the active Tilemap or mismatched pixels-per-unit. Ready to build a small platformer section step-by-step and understand the why behind each step?

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies. First, you will explain the purpose of Unity's Tilemap system and why a Grid plus Tilemap children is the right pattern for layered 2D scenes. For example, you will recognize why keeping background art on a separate Tilemap keeps sorting and draw order predictable. Second, you will create and manage Tile Palettes and generate Tile assets from a sliced tileset. You'll build a palette asset, drag sprites into it, and save each tile for painting. Third, you will paint and erase tiles to construct multi-layered levels and assign sorting layers so background and foreground render correctly. Practically, this reduces manual sprite placement and speeds iteration. Fourth, you will implement collision by adding TilemapCollider2D and then optimize it by enabling Used By Composite and adding a CompositeCollider2D, reducing per-tile colliders into a single shape. Each objective maps to a verified competency milestone so you can check your work. These skills matter because they let you iterate levels quickly, avoid common collision pitfalls, and keep performance manageable as your map grows.

These additional objectives focus on advanced Tilemap features and safe design practices. First, you will identify when to use Rule Tiles to automatically adapt sprites based on neighbors, such as auto-connecting terrain edges, which significantly reduces manual edge painting. A concrete example is a grass tile that switches to an edge sprite when no neighboring grass tile exists on the left. Second, you will create Animated Tiles for repeating motion like flowing water, assigning a sequence of sprites and an animation speed so the Tile animates in-game. Third, you will understand the role of Scriptable Tiles, and the basics of creating a custom tile class that inherits from TileBase, which is useful when you need custom placement logic or tile-triggered behavior. Fourth, you will learn practical safeguards: check Pixels Per Unit on your sliced sprites, confirm the active Tilemap before painting, set Sorting Layers, and save often to avoid accidental overwrites. Each of these skills improves speed, visual consistency, and runtime performance. Practice these milestones in the hands-on activity to lock in the workflow for production-ready 2D level design.

A Tilemap system is Unity's specialized workflow and set of components for building grid-based 2D levels by painting tiles rather than placing individual sprites. At its core, a Grid GameObject defines the overall grid layout — cell size and spacing — while Tilemap child GameObjects store tile data for specific layers like ground, background, or foreground. Each Tilemap has a Tilemap Renderer that draws its tiles and can be assigned to a Sorting Layer so rendering order is predictable. The practical benefit is huge: painting a repeated floor pattern, or adding decorative elements, becomes fast and consistent, and tiles can carry physics or animation. For example, in a platformer you might create one Tilemap called GroundTilemap for collision and another called BackgroundTilemap for parallax art; each uses the same Grid so alignment is consistent. A common misconception is treating Tilemaps like simple sprites; instead, think of them as data layers that combine visual sprites with optional runtime behavior such as colliders or scripted logic. Key takeaway: Tilemaps turn repetitive level construction into a paint workflow that keeps art, physics, and layering organized and easy to iterate.

Setting up a Grid and Tilemap children is the first practical step to paint a level that aligns perfectly. Start by creating a Grid GameObject via the editor's GameObject menu and choosing 2D Object → Tilemap. Unity creates a Grid with a Tilemap child and a Tilemap Renderer component. The Grid controls cell size and cell gap; for pixel-art tiles you typically set the Grid cell size to match your sprite's Pixels Per Unit so tiles snap neatly. Next, add additional Tilemap children for different layers: rename the default to GroundTilemap, then add another child and call it BackgroundTilemap. Use separate Tilemaps to control ordering and collisions; GroundTilemap will often host physics and colliders while BackgroundTilemap remains purely visual. A common error is painting on the Scene without the intended Tilemap selected in the Hierarchy; always confirm the active Tilemap before painting. Finally, set Sorting Layers on each Tilemap's Tilemap Renderer — for example, Background behind Platforms — so draw order is correct. Following this disciplined setup avoids alignment problems and keeps your project organized as levels grow. Creating a Grid and Tilemap Children means create grid → create tilemap children, rename layers, match cell size to pixels per unit, and set sorting layers for clear draw order.. In practical terms, step-by-step setup for consistent alignment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A Tile Palette is your toolbox of paintable tiles. To create one, open Window → 2D → Tile Palette and click Create New Palette. Name it, for example, PlatformerTiles, and save it as an asset in your project. Next, prepare your tileset by importing a tileset image, setting Sprite Mode to Multiple, and slicing it in the Sprite Editor using Grid By Cell Size. Make sure Pixels Per Unit matches your intended Grid cell size. Then drag the sliced sprites from the Project window into the Tile Palette window. Unity prompts you to save each sprite as a Tile asset; accept and save them. You can create Animated Tiles or Rule Tiles from the Create menu if you need motion or neighbor-aware sprites. A practical tip: group tiles in the palette by usage — terrain, decorations, hazards — so painting is faster. A common mistake is forgetting to save the Palette asset before painting; if the palette is not saved, tile assets might not be created persistently. By the end of this workflow you'll have a Palette populated with Tile assets, ready for the brush, fill, and erase tools in the Tile Palette window.

Painting a level is the tactile part of Tilemap design. The Tile Palette offers three primary tools you'll use constantly: the brush, fill, and erase tools. The brush paints individual tiles or click-drag strokes; use it for placing platforms and decorations precisely. The fill tool fills contiguous areas with the selected tile, which is handy for creating large ground masses quickly. The erase tool removes tiles from the active Tilemap. Always ensure the correct Tilemap is selected in the Hierarchy because painting acts on the active Tilemap — a very common error is painting on a different layer or seeing no change because an inactive Tilemap was selected. When you paint ground tiles intended for collisions, remember to add the TilemapCollider2D to that Tilemap; painting more tiles will update the collider set. Another practical tip: use smaller brush sizes for details and the fill tool for the broad strokes, then erase where needed to shape platforms. After painting, run the game to validate that the player interacts with the painted ground as expected; if not, check that the Tilemap has a collider and that the Sorting Layer is correct. Try painting a small platform, add TilemapCollider2D, and jump on it to confirm behavior.

When you want physics interactions with your painted ground, add a TilemapCollider2D component to the Tilemap GameObject that holds those tiles. The TilemapCollider2D inspects the tiles painted on its Tilemap and creates per-tile colliders, typically box-shaped, so a Rigidbody2D-based player can stand on or collide with them. This automatic generation is convenient but can become costly for large contiguous areas because it produces many individual colliders. One common pitfall is forgetting to add this component to the ground Tilemap and wondering why the player falls through. Another pitfall is leaving many individual colliders active in a large level, which increases physics workload. The recommended pattern is to enable Used By Composite on the TilemapCollider2D and then add a CompositeCollider2D to the same GameObject; Unity will then merge many small colliders into a single composite shape, drastically reducing physics overhead. Implementation note: adding a CompositeCollider2D often requires adding a Rigidbody2D and setting it to Static so the composite shape participates correctly. Always test performance after painting large areas and consider chunking very large worlds into multiple scenes to keep physics manageable.

Understanding the trade-offs between per-tile colliders and a CompositeCollider2D is essential for performance. By default, TilemapCollider2D generates an individual collider for each painted tile. This is simple and flexible, but on large contiguous ground areas it can create thousands of colliders, increasing physics calculations and reducing frame rate. The alternative is to check Used By Composite on the TilemapCollider2D and add a CompositeCollider2D. The composite merges those many colliders into larger contiguous shapes, dramatically reducing the number of collision checks. However, the composite shape can be slightly less accurate for isolated small tiles or tile-by-tile interactions that depend on per-tile segmentation. A practical guideline: use per-tile colliders during early prototyping for clarity, but switch to CompositeCollider2D for solid ground layers in larger or performance-sensitive levels. Also remember to set the Rigidbody2D to Static on the GameObject with the CompositeCollider2D. A common mistake is enabling composite but forgetting to check Used By Composite, which leaves the many per-tile colliders active. Test your level: if you see physics stutter on large maps, the composite is likely the right solution. Per-tile colliders vs CompositeCollider2D means per-tile colliders are simple and precise; compositecollider2d reduces collider count and improves performance for large, contiguous surfaces.. In practical terms, performance trade-offs and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Rule Tiles let you define neighbor-based rules so a tile chooses the correct sprite depending on surrounding tiles. Instead of placing different edge or corner sprites manually, you create a Rule Tile and define rules like: use the center sprite when surrounded, use an edge sprite when no neighbor exists on the left, or use a corner sprite in L-shaped configurations. This automation is extremely useful for terrain that must visually connect, such as grass meeting dirt or stone paths. A concrete example: a grass Rule Tile might show a full grass tile when there are grass neighbors on all sides but automatically switch to a left-edge sprite when there is no grass to the left. Rule Tiles accelerate painting because the correct sprite is chosen at paint time based on local context. A common misconception is that Rule Tiles limit control — in fact, they increase consistency and reduce human error, while still allowing manual override if you need a special tile placement. Use Rule Tiles for large areas with repeating connection logic and save time while keeping art consistent across the map.

Animated Tiles let you assign a sequence of sprites and an animation speed so a tile cycles through frames in the Tilemap. This is ideal for water, lava, torches, or any surface that should exhibit simple looping motion. To create one, use Create → 2D → Tiles → Animated Tile, then assign a set of sprites and a speed parameter. When painted, the Animated Tile will render its frame sequence at runtime without requiring separate Animator objects or spritesheets. Use Animated Tiles sparingly on large maps because many animated tiles can increase rendering work; reserve them for surfaces that benefit from motion. An example: create an Animated Tile for a water tile with three sprites and a moderate speed so the water appears to flow. A misconception is that animated tiles are heavy like full skeletal animations — they are simple sprite swaps driven by the Tile asset and are efficient for many common cases. The takeaway: Animated Tiles give motion without additional animator overhead, but monitor performance if you animate many tiles simultaneously. Animated Tiles & Bringing Levels to Life means animated tiles cycle sprite frames at a set speed, giving simple motion like flowing water without extra animator components.. Scriptable Tiles let you implement custom placement or runtime behavior by creating a C# class that inherits from TileBase. This is an advanced technique for cases where a tile must perform logic when placed, removed, or when an actor interacts with it — for example, a pressure plate tile that triggers an event when the player stands on it. The chapter notes that you can create your own C# scripts inheriting from TileBase; do this carefully because custom code introduces maintenance and compatibility concerns. A minimal safe example is defining a class header that inherits TileBase and then implementing only the methods you need for drawing or providing tile data. Avoid embedding heavy runtime logic directly in tile data; prefer raising events that other components handle. An important practical step is testing your Scriptable Tile in the editor by placing and removing instances to confirm behavior and saving frequently. Misconception check: Scriptable Tiles are not required for most projects — use them only when the built-in Tile types (Tile, Rule Tile, Animated Tile) cannot express the behavior you need. This hands-on activity walks you through building a small platformer section with Tilemaps. Start from a project with a sliced tileset saved as PlatformerTileset. png and ensure sprites are sliced with the expected Pixels Per Unit. Step 1: Create a Grid and a Tilemap child via GameObject → 2D Object → Tilemap. Rename the child GroundTilemap. Step 2: Add another Tilemap child named BackgroundTilemap and set Sorting Layers: Background for background, Platforms for ground. Step 3: Open Window → 2D → Tile Palette. Create a new palette named PlatformerTiles and drag your sliced sprites into it, saving Tile assets when prompted. Step 4: Select GroundTilemap and paint a simple ground base with the brush or fill tool, then add a few floating platforms. Step 5: Add a TilemapCollider2D to GroundTilemap, check Used By Composite, then add a CompositeCollider2D and accept creating a Rigidbody2D set to Static. Step 6: Select BackgroundTilemap and paint background elements. Step 7: Play the scene to verify the player can stand and jump on the painted ground. Checkpoints: verify PPU alignment, active Tilemap selection before painting, and that Collider + Composite settings improve physics. Save frequently.

Let's summarize the essential concepts you should remember. First, the Tilemap System: a workflow that uses a Grid and Tilemap children to paint and manage layered 2D levels, enabling consistent alignment and faster iteration. Second, the Tile Palette and Tile Asset: the Tile Palette is the editor window that stores paintable Tile assets generated from sliced sprites; these tiles are what you paint onto Tilemaps. Third, TilemapCollider2D and CompositeCollider2D: TilemapCollider2D generates per-tile colliders automatically, and CompositeCollider2D merges those colliders when Used By Composite is enabled to improve physics performance. Keep these three ideas in mind as touchstones when building levels — they govern how you paint, render, and make the level physically interactive. A quick test to verify understanding is to paint a platform, add TilemapCollider2D, enable composite optimization, and confirm your player can stand on it without performance drops.

Here are three advanced concepts to remember. Rule Tiles automate sprite selection based on neighboring tiles, which gives seamless edges and corners without manual placement. Animated Tiles let you define sprite sequences and speeds for motion like flowing water or flickering lights directly in the Tile asset, keeping animation simple and efficient. Scriptable Tiles allow custom C# logic by inheriting from TileBase to implement specialized placement or interactive behaviors, but they carry maintenance costs and should be used only when built-in tile types aren't sufficient. Together these features let you automate visuals, add life, and extend tile behavior when necessary. A closing question: which combination of these tile types best fits your next level — Rule Tiles for terrain flow, Animated Tiles for environmental life, and Scriptable Tiles for bespoke interactions?
